assessment.nobel_worthiness: The detection of a diffuse flux of astrophysical neutrinos in the TeV-PeV range, followed by evidence for neutrino emission from the blazar TXS 0506+056 and the Galactic plane, opened a new observational window. It required instrumenting a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice, a bold and original detector concept, and it is a clean, lasting discovery of the kind I know well from astroparticle instrumentation.
assessment.attribution: IceCube is a large collaboration, so any prize must credit the idea and leadership rather than the whole team. The supplied credit offers only Francis Halzen as the conceptual and organisational driver of the instrument. A single-name configuration is legitimate but leaves out other contributors to the detector concept and to the early AMANDA work. I rely on my own knowledge for this and have not verified it independently.
assessment.maturity: The diffuse astrophysical flux has been confirmed in several independent channels, and the source identifications have grown steadily. Complementary results from KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD provide some independent support. Timing looks appropriate and the interpretation of the flux is stable.
uncertainties: A one-person laureate list may under-represent a collaboration-scale discovery and other instrument builders.
The origin of most of the diffuse flux is still unresolved, though the existence of the flux is secure.
Whether the committee prefers the discovery or the source-identification result as the cited achievement.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Measuring the last unknown neutrino mixing angle theta-13 with reactor antineutrinos was a precise, decisive experiment. It opened the way to CP-violation searches and mass-ordering studies in the lepton sector. The experimental design was clever, with near and far detectors cancelling systematic uncertainties, and the result is a good example of careful accelerator-style discipline applied at reactors.
assessment.attribution: The credited names fit a natural three-person configuration spanning the leaders of Daya Bay (Wang and Luk) and RENO (Kim). Double Chooz is not represented, and T2K's earlier electron-neutrino appearance hint also played a role, so some credit questions remain. I would keep all three names.
assessment.maturity: The result has been confirmed by multiple experiments and refined to a precision of a few per cent. The picture is stable and well integrated into the three-flavour framework. Recognition is timely, as the Nobel Prize in Physics 2015 already covered neutrino oscillations and this is a clear follow-on.
uncertainties: Possible dispute over priority and inclusion of Double Chooz and T2K contributors.
The committee may feel the 2015 oscillation prize already covers the field.
I am relying on memory for the sequence of announcements in 2011 and 2012.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators, combined with the experimental discovery of the effect in HgTe quantum wells, created a whole field. The idea is original and conceptually clear, linked to a measurable quantised conductance, and it has driven fifteen years of work on topological materials.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical step. Molenkamp led the experimental demonstration in HgTe, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction, who are not in the supplied credit. That omission is a real allocation problem. The three credited names make a plausible theory-plus-experiment prize, but some fairness issues remain.
assessment.maturity: Many independent confirmations exist, including three-dimensional topological insulators and extensions to other materials. The interpretation is stable. Recognition is well within the timely window, though the Nobel committee already honoured topological phase transitions in 2016.
uncertainties: Exclusion of Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang from the supplied credit, along with other early contributors.
Overlap with the 2016 prize on topological phases.
Whether the experimental realisation is a sufficient component or the prize should be theory-only.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction of flat bands at a magic twist angle and the later discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene created moire quantum materials as a tunable platform. The combination of a clear theoretical prediction and a striking experiment is attractive, and the impact on condensed-matter physics has been large and rapid.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the key prediction. Jarillo-Herrero led the discovery experiments, along with Cory Dean's group and others in follow-on work. The credited trio forms a clean prediction and discovery pairing, though experimental co-credit with a first-author student is a typical complication, and others may contend for a place.
assessment.maturity: Results have been replicated by many groups, but the mechanism of superconductivity in the system is still debated. Relatively young for a prize, but the observation is secure. It is a case where the observation is mature even if the theory of the phases is not.
uncertainties: Origin of the superconductivity is not settled.
Possible premature recognition given the field is only about seven years old.
Unclear whether other early theorists, such as Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto, deserve credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The optical lattice clock, with its magic-wavelength trapping idea, brought fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and created a new generation of time standards. It is a precision-measurement instrument with clear impact on metrology, tests of fundamental physics and geodesy, and the concept is original and cleanly stated.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic wavelength lattice concept, and Ye's group realised outstanding clock performance with strontium. The two-name configuration is natural. Ye also appears on other candidates, which creates a possible overlap with other recognition, and others who contributed to lattice clock work could be considered.
assessment.maturity: Many groups worldwide have reproduced the performance, and the redefinition of the second is in progress. The concept is well confirmed. Timing is good, even if one might wait for the redefinition to become official.
uncertainties: Possible competing claims from other lattice clock groups and from ion-clock workers.
Overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes on frequency combs and ion control.
Whether the committee would prefer to wait for the formal redefinition of the second.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution links the foundations of quantum mechanics to a practical technology. The BB84 protocol and Ekert's entanglement-based protocol are original and conceptually simple, with a lasting impact on quantum information science and a good bridge from fundamental ideas to applications.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard introduced BB84, and Ekert introduced the E91 scheme using Bell inequalities. The credited trio is a recognised grouping. Wiesner's earlier conjugate-coding idea is not in the credited list, which raises a historical fairness question I cannot resolve from the supplied evidence.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations are widespread, including satellite links, and the theory is well developed. However, practical security against real device imperfections is still an active topic. The 2022 prize already recognised entanglement experiments, which is related.
uncertainties: Wiesner's role and the question of whether the credit should be three people or two.
Overlap with the 2022 prize on Bell tests and quantum information.
Question of physics versus information-science character of the discovery.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Kilonovae link neutron-star mergers to heavy-element synthesis and gravitational-wave multimessenger astronomy. The combination of prediction and the observation following GW170817 is a compelling demonstration, and it ties into astrophysical nucleosynthesis and the multimessenger programme I am close to.
assessment.attribution: Metzger and Kasen made major theoretical predictions, with Li and Paczynski's earlier idea also relevant, and Tanvir contributed to the afterglow observation linked to GRB 130603B. The credited trio omits Li and Paczynski, and the observation of AT2017gfo was made by many teams, so credit is spread and hard to allocate.
assessment.maturity: The AT2017gfo event is a single well-observed case, with a few further candidates. Interpretation of the heavy-element yield is still evolving. The result is solid but rests on one major event, so the recognition might be a little early.
uncertainties: Only one gravitational-wave associated event is clearly confirmed.
Complex credit among theorists and the many observing teams.
The detailed composition and the relative role of r-process sites remain open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Evidence for a nanohertz gravitational-wave background from pulsar timing arrays is a new observational window on supermassive black-hole binaries or exotic early-universe sources. The measurement builds on decades of precise pulsar timing and is of high potential importance.
assessment.attribution: Pulsar timing array work was driven by NANOGrav, EPTA, PPTA, and others. The supplied names represent leaders across the different collaborations, but no single configuration clearly captures the decisive contributors, and other individuals such as Foster, Backer and Hellings and Downs could be argued for. Attribution is therefore unresolved.
assessment.maturity: The evidence is a few sigma and is consistent across several arrays, but it falls short of a definitive detection and the source of the signal is not established. This is premature for a prize, so I rank it last of my eight.
uncertainties: Detection significance remains short of the conventional discovery threshold.
Astrophysical versus cosmological origin of the signal is open.
Credit is spread across several large collaborations with unclear leaders.
